nameStory: This moth gets its name from the distinctive dark bars and twin spots that decorate its wings like a carefully woven carpet pattern. The 'twin-spot' refers to paired circular markings on each wing, while the dark bars create intricate geometric designs reminiscent of traditional floor coverings.
description: The Dark-barred Twin-spot Carpet is a medium-sized moth in the geometer family, known for their distinctive looping caterpillar movement. Adults have intricately patterned wings with a wingspan of about 1 to 1.5 inches, featuring complex geometric designs in browns, grays, and muted earth tones. The forewings display the characteristic dark crossbars and paired circular spots that give this species its common name. Like other geometers, the caterpillars are 'inchworms' that arch their bodies as they crawl.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive twin circular spots on each forewing, accompanied by dark zigzag crossbars that create a carpet-like geometric pattern in muted browns and grays

idTips.label: Wing Position at Rest
idTips.description: Wings held horizontally outward from the body when at rest, creating a triangular silhouette typical of geometer moths

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a wingspan of 1 to 1.5 inches, larger than many micro-moths but smaller than sphinx moths

idTips.label: Body Build
idTips.description: Slender body relative to wing size, with a delicate appearance and thread-like antennae that feel smooth to gentle touch

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a somewhat erratic, fluttering pattern typical of geometers, often attracted to lights on warm evenings

habitat: Found throughout New England in a variety of habitats including woodland edges, gardens, parks, and areas with mixed vegetation. They're particularly common in areas with bedstraw and other low-growing plants that serve as host plants for their caterpillars. Look for them in both suburban and rural settings, from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with fresh individuals appearing from May onward. Look for them at porch lights and outdoor fixtures on mild evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season when adults are most active and numerous. Moths are attracted to lights and can be found resting on walls, tree trunks, and vegetation during the day.
seasonality.fall: Second generation adults may appear in early fall in warmer years. Caterpillars are actively feeding and preparing for winter as inchworms on low plants.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as pupae in the soil or leaf litter. No adult activity during cold months, but pupae can occasionally be found when gardening or raking.

funFact: Despite being called a 'carpet' moth, this species has absolutely nothing to do with household carpets - it can't survive indoors and has never been known to damage fabrics, unlike clothes moths which are in a completely different family!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other carpet moths in the same family, but the combination of twin spots and dark crossbars is distinctive. Remember: 'Twin spots plus dark bars equals carpet star' - no other local geometer has this exact combination of paired circular markings with prominent zigzag crossbands.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'carpet moth' often confuses people who worry about fabric damage, but these are outdoor moths that pose no threat to household items. The 'carpet' refers only to their wing patterns resembling woven designs, not their habitat or diet.
compareHints: As the only Xanthorhoe species commonly found in New England, it's most easily confused with other carpet moths in the Geometridae family. However, most other carpets lack the distinctive paired circular spots, having instead single eyespots, solid bands, or completely different geometric patterns. The twin-spot feature combined with the dark crossbars makes this species relatively easy to identify among New England's geometer moths.
